content: 1. Vaccination schedules for hepatitis B include doses administered at 0, 1-2, and 4 months, as well as at 0, 12, and 24 months. 2. The adult dose of Recombivax-HB (10 µg), when given in a 2-dose schedule to children and adolescents aged 11-15 years at 0 and 4-6 months, produces antibody levels comparable to those achieved with the 5-µg dose administered in a 3-dose schedule. 3. However, there is no available data on the long-term persistence of antibodies or protection for 2-dose schedules. 4. No combination vaccines containing the hepatitis B vaccine antigen are approved for use in adolescents aged 11-17 years. 5. Deviations from the standard minimum spacing of vaccine doses do not appear to affect immunogenicity significantly. 6. Extending the interval between the first two doses has minimal impact on immunogenicity or final antibody concentrations. 7. 8. Longer intervals between the last two doses result in higher final antibody levels but may increase the risk of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in individuals with delayed vaccine responses. 9. No differences in immunogenicity have been observed when doses of hepatitis B vaccine from different manufacturers are used in the same vaccination series. 10. Higher vaccine doses may be more immunogenic, but no specific recommendations have been made regarding this. 11. Dialysis formulations of the hepatitis B vaccine are administered on a 3-dose schedule at 0, 1, and 6 months. 12. For certain cases, two 1.0-mL doses may be administered at one site on a 4-dose schedule at 0, 1, 2, and 6 months. 13. Infants born to hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg)-positive mothers who do not respond to a primary vaccine series have shown satisfactory responses to a repeat 3-dose revaccination series, provided they are not infected with HBV. 14. There is no evidence to suggest that children who fail to develop detectable antibodies after six vaccine doses would benefit from additional doses. 15. Preterm infants weighing less than 2,000 grams at birth exhibit a reduced response to hepatitis B vaccination if administered before one month of age. 16. By one month of age, medically stable preterm infants, regardless of birth weight or gestational age, respond to vaccination similarly to full-term infants. 17. Data on the response of pediatric hemodialysis patients to standard pediatric vaccine doses are limited, but protective antibody levels are achieved in 75%-97% of those receiving higher doses (20 µg) on either a 3or 4-dose schedule. 18. Immunocompromised children and adolescents, such as those undergoing chemotherapy, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, or living with HIV, also exhibit reduced humoral responses to hepatitis B vaccination. 19. Modified dosing regimens, such as doubling the standard antigen dose or administering additional doses, may improve response rates, though data on these alternative schedules are limited. 20. Anti-HBs is the only measurable correlate of vaccine-induced protection. 21. 22. 23. After primary immunization with the hepatitis B vaccine, anti-HBs concentrations decline rapidly within the first year and more slowly thereafter. 24. Among children who respond to a primary vaccine series with antibody levels greater than 10 mIU/mL, 15%-50% experience a loss of detectable anti-HBs levels 5-15 years after vaccination. 25. 26. Despite declines in anti-HBs levels to below 10 mIU/mL, nearly all vaccinated individuals remain protected against HBV infection due to the preservation of immune memory. 27. Immune memory is thought to be maintained through the selective expansion and differentiation of antigen-specific B and T lymphocyte clones. 28. Studies have demonstrated the persistence of vaccine-induced immune memory in individuals vaccinated during childhood, even 13-23 years later, as evidenced by an anamnestic increase in anti-HBs levels following an additional vaccine dose. 29. 30. Cohort studies of immunocompetent individuals vaccinated as children or infants indicate that nearly all who respond to a primary series remain protected from HBV infection, even after antibody loss. 31. No clinical cases of hepatitis B have been observed in follow-up studies conducted 15-20 years after vaccination among immunocompetent individuals with initial antibody levels greater than 10 mIU/mL. 32. Breakthrough infections, identified by the presence of anti-HBc or HBV DNA, have been documented in a small percentage of vaccinated individuals, but these infections are typically transient and asymptomatic. Chronic infections are rare. 33. Breakthrough infections resulting in chronic infection have only been observed among vaccinated infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers. 34. Limited data exist on the duration of immune memory after hepatitis B vaccination in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV, undergoing dialysis, chemotherapy, or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. 35. No clinically significant HBV infections have been documented among immunocompromised individuals who maintain protective levels of anti-HBs. 36. 37. HBIG alone has also been shown to be effective in preventing HBV transmission, but with the availability of the hepatitis B vaccine, HBIG is typically used as an adjunct.
